Where Gemini 4 Argon fails

Across the 22 samples, Gemini 4 Argon did not pass 39 of its 65 graded runs and passed the other 26. We sorted the failures into five failure modes. Each sample is counted once, under its main failure mode, though single runs can fail in different ways.

39 of 65
Argon runs not passed
35%
Argon pass@1
57%
Argon pass@2
Failure modeDetails and examplesRuns not passedSamples
Workflow and access failuresMissed cleanup, conflict handling or permitted access during a workflow.
  • Cancelled upload: Cancelling an upload should free its reserved space. Argon's version kept the space occupied, so the next upload was rejected as over quota.
  • Overlapping upload and delete: A valid package upload should still finish when a delete overlaps with it. Argon's version rejected the upload as a conflict.
  • Download permissions: A scanner should be allowed to download from its assigned repository. Argon's security change blocked that permitted download.
156
Incorrect data or stateLost values, changed future behavior or missed database-change notifications.
  • Saving and reopening a frequency counter: After reopening, the counter used a different random sequence, so it no longer continued identically when given the same new inputs.
  • Adding CSV support: The data-processing tool should preserve correct summary totals. Argon's changes produced a count of 75 matching records where 119 were expected.
  • Restoring an older database: Restoration should preserve values in columns added later. Argon's version lost those values when restoring an older-format database.
64
Incomplete ports and rebuildsFailed to preserve the original behavior across inputs or deliver a program that builds.
  • Porting a counting library: Ordinary counts worked, but the largest supported count failed in one storage format. The port should match the original at that limit.
  • Rebuilding a video encoder: Argon selected from fixed encoded samples, which could not handle the wider range of video inputs. Only 32 of 453 checks passed.
  • Porting a graph library: Duplicate functions and incompatible function calls stopped the submitted code from compiling, so none of the behavior checks could run.
53
Missing required behaviorPassed many checks while missing required modes, interfaces or processing paths.
  • Combining image filters: Argon's repair still failed when inclusion and exclusion filters were used together. Only images allowed by both rules should be processed.
  • Fixing incorrect experiment results: Failed training runs were being reported as zero loss. Argon reproduced the bug, but its fix covered only two of four tested variants.
64
Unfinished integration and featuresLeft configuration dependencies, module connections or requested API options incomplete.
  • Changing a deployment's project name: Generated machine startup scripts still contained the old project name. The setting should have updated everywhere it was used.
  • Splitting infrastructure into modules: The top-level configuration still read outputs from the old resources, rather than from the new modules as required.
  • Adding XML options: New options were meant to control null values and whitespace. Argon's submitted library rejected both options as unrecognized arguments.
75
Total3922

Headroom for improvement

On the 21 samples with two or more graded Argon runs, the chance that one run passes (pass@1) is 35%, and the chance that at least one of two runs passes (pass@2) is 57%, with each sample weighted equally. Argon can often reach a working solution but does not get there reliably.

Argon often implements much of the solution, but misses conditions that matter in real use: cancelling an upload, restoring older data, combining settings, or keeping totals correct after a change. More training examples covering these situations can help strengthen that behavior. These environments provide concrete failure cases, realistic implementation work, and executable checks to measure whether the gaps are closing.

Executive summary

283
Tasks
39%
Gemini 4 Argon pass rate
1%

Each task asks the agent to make software behave exactly like a reference version. In the reimplementation tasks the agent writes a new program from scratch, in a language of its choice, from a reference program and its documentation. In the upgrade tasks the agent brings an existing repository up to the reference's newer release by changing its code. In the migration tasks the agent ports a Java or Rust library to Go or C++ behind fixed signatures. In 26% of tasks the agent chooses the language; the most common fixed languages are Go (29%) and C (17%).

Gemini 4 Argon passes 39% of its runs and fails every run on 27% of them. Gemini 3.8 Flash passes 1% of its runs and fails every run on 96% of them.

Why this catalog

Problems engineers face

Engineers often have to make software behave exactly like a version they cannot reuse: rebuilding a tool whose source is unavailable, bringing an old codebase up to a newer release, or replacing a Java or Rust dependency with a port in Go or C++. In each case the specification is observable behaviour. The hard part is inferring the rules from outputs and documentation, then matching exit codes, output, file effects, numeric precision and result ordering without seeing the tests.

How the tasks reproduce them

Every task runs offline, and hidden tests compare the result with the reference. In reimplementation and upgrade tasks the reference is a program the agent can run but not read. For a reimplementation, the agent writes a source project and a compile.sh from the reference and its documentation. For an upgrade, the agent changes an existing repository in /app/repo, which is built with a fixed /opt/task/build.sh. Migration tasks provide the original source and a skeleton with final signatures, and most add a mig-check tool.

Typical prompts

  • Reproduce the documented behaviour of an execute-only program, delivered as source code plus compile.sh.
  • Update an existing repository to match a reference program, after first writing a research and plan file.
  • Port a named Java or Rust library to Go or C++ from a reference folder, keeping the given signatures, within per-test time and memory limits.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)

We're moving a dependency from Java to Go, and I need a Go port of the dynatrace-oss/dynahist library. The Java source is in /app/java_reference/. I've already laid out the Go package in /app/port/: every type and function our code calls is there with its final signature, but the bodies are just stubs. Could you fill in the implementation so it behaves exactly like the Java library?

When you're done, I'll run the library's own test suite, ported to Go, against /app/port. I'm not including those tests here, so please work from the Java source itself and match it closely: error cases, edge cases, numeric precision and the order things come back in.

A few things that will save you some pain:

  • Keep the signatures and the package name in /app/port as they are; our callers use them as-is. Edit the existing files in place and declare each type and function once.
  • Run mig-check (on the PATH) often. It compares /app/port with the original stubs, runs go build and go vet, and flags package-level names that clash with our test helpers (they start with mig or Mig).
  • Go's regexp is RE2, so Java-only syntax such as the (?u) flag, back-references, look-around and \u{...} escapes makes a package-level regexp.MustCompile panic at start-up.
  • This package ends up inside a sandboxed service, so every non-test .go file under /app/port must stay off os, os/exec, syscall, runtime, plugin, net, net/http, net/rpc, io/ioutil, embed, unsafe, flag or testing (and anything under testing/), cgo, and the //go:linkname and //go:embed directives. Write the logic yourself rather than calling out to another program; the rest of the standard library is fine.
  • Our test machine has 2 vCPUs, and each test gets 60 seconds and a 2 GB address-space limit, so keep things reasonably efficient.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)
Task context

Reproduce the documented behavior of the program in this workspace. The reference program is /opt/task-reference/executable. Its bundled documentation is available in the workspace. The task runs model commands as the non-root agent user. The reference is execute-only for that user, so it can be run but not read, copied, hard-linked, or recovered through /proc. A root model shell means the task platform did not honor the declared user and is not part of the task contract.

Required result

Write a source code project and an executable ./compile.sh. Running ./compile.sh on a fresh checkout must produce ./executable in the workspace root. The rebuilt executable must match the reference program's observable behavior, including output, exit codes, and file system effects.

You may choose the implementation language and design. You can learn the behavior from the bundled documentation and by running the reference program.

The grader checks only your submission's fresh offline build and its observable behavior. It does not assess your implementation language or how you learned the behavior. Do not include the reference executable's bytes in the submission under another name or embedded inside another file. Do not read or inspect the grader harness, hidden tests, or recorded expectations, even if a platform defect makes them accessible. During grading, the internet, package registries, the reference program, and system copies of the same tool are unavailable. Your build and executable must work without them.

Reusable input assets

When /workspace/assets exists, it contains hard-to-create reusable inputs such as media, archives, databases, or custom binary files. You may inspect, copy, or modify these inputs while recreating the program. Ordinary source and text inputs are not provided and should be created as needed.

How your work is scored

Your executable is graded by replaying many recorded behaviors of the reference program against it and scoring the fraction that match. A match always requires the same exit code and the same file system effects. Plain output and ordinary files are compared byte for byte. JSON output and JSON files are normally compared as parsed values, so insignificant whitespace and object key order do not matter unless the documentation makes formatting or ordering part of the behavior. SQLite files are compared by their logical contents. Terminal progress output is compared by its final visible text. A recorded behavior can require exact bytes when formatting or ordering is part of the documented behavior. Partial credit is the norm, so every additional behavior you match raises your score, and there is no bonus for finishing early.

Coverage to aim for

Grading samples behavior from the documented interface. Only behavior that can be tested reliably in a bounded offline run is graded.

When applicable, support:

  • commands, subcommands, options, aliases, and short forms
  • representative documented values
  • help and version output
  • standard input, files, and directories
  • configuration files and environment variables
  • standard output, standard error, exit codes, and file system effects
  • error handling
  • empty, non-ASCII, binary, and unusually named inputs

The test suite may not cover every documented behavior.

Using the reference program

Run /opt/task-reference/executable to observe the reference. The file is outside the submitted workspace and is unavailable during grading. Your ./compile.sh can therefore write ./executable without replacing the reference while you work.

Before you finish

Passing tests you wrote yourself is not evidence that you are done. Before you stop:

  1. list every option and subcommand in the reference program's help output;
  2. for each one, run /opt/task-reference/executable and your executable on the same input and compare output using the scoring rules above, along with the exit code and files written;
  3. fix every disagreement you find, then repeat from step 1.

Stop when no disagreement remains or when your budget is spent, whichever comes first.

Each task changes a production system that must keep running. In the system design tasks the agent makes a multi-process service hold its guarantees through crashes, retries, races and returning stale writers. In the infrastructure tasks the agent restructures live Terraform or Pulumi code so that the plan against production state changes nothing that is deployed. The main languages are HCL (Terraform) (63%), Python (11%) and Go (10%).

Gemini 4 Argon passes 20% of its runs and fails every run on 44% of them. Gemini 3.8 Flash passes 12% of its runs and fails every run on 69% of them.

Why this catalog

Problems engineers face

Production systems fail in specific ways when they change while running. In services where several processes share state and any of them can stop, the failures are duplicate effects after retries, lost notifications, stale writers returning after a takeover, limits that hold in one process but not across instances, and partial state after a crash. In infrastructure code, a flat Terraform stack has to become modules with stable keys, or move to Pulumi, while every deployed resource stays exactly as it is.

How the tasks reproduce them

Both kinds of task give the agent a working copy of the system and grade the result with hidden checks after the session. Service tasks pin an open-source repository at a base commit, with a short specification that often sets time limits. The agent runs the needed databases, caches or brokers locally and delivers a patch. Hidden tests then kill or pause processes and confirm existing behaviour still works. Infrastructure tasks ship the stack with its recorded production state. A verifier plans the result with refresh disabled, expects moves only, then plans hidden changes such as an added key.

Typical prompts

  • A capability gap stated as "X cannot do Y", followed by measurable requirements, many with time limits.
  • A closing paragraph with the repository path, how to start each service and the build command.
  • A first-person request to modularize a named production Terraform stack, followed by rules for modules, for_each keys, variables, outputs and banned constructs.

Domain breakdown

The tasks span nine domains. The largest, State-preserving infrastructure changes, makes up 64% of the catalog.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)
Checkpoint the budget sync log

We need the sync server to compact a budget's history from a client-built snapshot while keeping its sync group stable, so long-lived budgets stay small without offline devices losing edits; the server cannot inspect encrypted changes. Today it retains every change indefinitely, and resetting sync shrinks a budget only by replacing its group, which makes offline devices lose edits they have not uploaded.

What we need
  • Configure the message-count threshold with ACTUAL_SYNC_CHECKPOINT_THRESHOLD (use 300 for this workload); below it no checkpoint is taken. After repeated transaction edits exceed it, two sync() calls leave no more than 300 server messages. A fresh download has the same transactions, payees, categories and budget amounts, and its local CRDT log contains at most one message per distinct cell.
  • Extend SyncRequest with checkpointId (protobuf field 7) and SyncResponse with checkpointWanted, checkpointRequired and checkpointBase (fields 3, 4 and 6); retain the existing protobuf fields. File info exposes messageCount, checkpointId and checkpointBase; its checkpointBase is the current receive base as a decimal string, the value a client sends in X-ACTUAL-CHECKPOINT-BASE to checkpoint everything received so far. The receive base tracks received changes, including late arrivals with older timestamps. A client builds a compact snapshot after syncing and commits it with POST /sync/commit-checkpoint, sending X-ACTUAL-FILE-ID, X-ACTUAL-GROUP-ID, X-ACTUAL-CHECKPOINT-BASE, X-ACTUAL-CHECKPOINT-ID, X-ACTUAL-CHECKPOINT-MERKLE and an application/encrypted-file body. A successful commit replaces the downloadable file with the snapshot and updates the checkpoint ID; the commit succeeds only when its receive base and prior checkpoint still match, otherwise it returns 409. A malformed receive base returns 400. A successful commit removes every change the checkpoint covers, and only those.
  • A disconnected device's unsent edits survive rejoining after a checkpoint, and its data converges with active and newly downloaded devices after two syncs. Repeated syncs after late, older-timestamp arrivals do not error, reset the group or discard changes. Concurrent checkpoint proposals install only one snapshot without surfacing a sync error.
  • A truncated or interrupted checkpoint body leaves both the message log and downloadable file unchanged; a later valid checkpoint can succeed. Old-format requests needing pruned history receive HTTP 400 with file-has-reset, not partial data; old-format requests already past the checkpoint continue normal sync. New clients needing the checkpoint receive checkpointRequired without losing unsent work.
Keep working

Existing /sync/sync, /sync/upload-user-file, /sync/download-user-file, /sync/get-user-file-info and password login remain usable.

Setup

Work in /app (Node 22, Yarn 4); build the affected packages with yarn workspace @actual-app/crdt build && yarn workspace @actual-app/core build && yarn workspace @actual-app/sync-server build && yarn workspace @actual-app/api build. Grading runs the packages as you leave them built in /app, without rebuilding, so rebuild after your last change. The sync server runs via node packages/sync-server/build/app.js, with SQLite files in ACTUAL_DATA_DIR and ACTUAL_USER_FILES. No Docker daemon or internet access is available inside the container.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)

Harbor's vulnerability scans currently create nonexpiring, project-wide scanner robots and submit their secrets in jobservice parameters, which remain in Redis job stats. Replace that lifecycle for IMAGE_SCAN jobs started by the artifact scan API and scan-on-push.

  • A scanner's credential, used directly (Basic) or exchanged at /service/token for a bearer token, gives only pull access to the scanned artifact's repository: no push anywhere, and no pull or push on any other repository in the same or another project. Scans started concurrently through two core instances each get a credential limited to their own repository.
  • A credential keeps working while a scan runs for three minutes, and successful scans still publish their vulnerability reports to the artifact. Existing scanner adapters using Basic or Bearer registry authorization continue to work.
  • After the task becomes final, Basic authentication using its credential is rejected with 401 or 403 by /v2/ and /service/token within 30 seconds. If jobservice is killed mid-scan without a final hook, within two minutes the credential is rejected with 401 or 403 by /v2/ and any robot account created for it is deleted. A scan requested through the artifact scan API while jobservice is down leaves no robot account behind.
  • Neither Redis keys and values nor GET /api/v1/jobs/{id} expose a scanner credential secret during or after a scan. Job parameters and the core and jobservice logs must not carry it either.
  • Preserve the existing artifact scan response and jobservice status API.

Work in /app (src/ is the Go module). PostgreSQL and Redis are installed; start them with sudo service postgresql start and sudo service redis-server start. Build offline from /app/src with GOPROXY=off go build ./core ./jobservice; generated Swagger server packages are present. Docker is unavailable inside the agent container. SBOM, scan-all, scanner registration and proxy-cache scanning are outside this change.

Prompt

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)

Two BaGetter instances sharing PostgreSQL and an S3 bucket can accept conflicting package-version writes: the database describes one upload while the bucket serves another. An interrupted push leaves unowned objects, and a failed prerelease overwrite can remove the previous package.

To close this out:

  • Coordinate version writes across instances so one of two different simultaneous pushes receives 201, while the loser does not; downloads, nuspecs, registration metadata and the flat-container index agree with the winner. A delayed S3 PUT from a writer whose database claim has expired must never replace the winner's served bytes or delete its objects. Storage:WriteClaimTimeoutSeconds defines the maximum database-disconnection window (3 seconds in the deployment).
  • An interrupted push remains invisible; a failed overwrite keeps the old prerelease bytes and metadata available until a successful replacement commits. Hard deletion must return 204 only when the version ends absent with no objects under packages/{id}/{version}/, or 404 when it remains downloadable. Concurrent cold mirror requests for the same upstream version both download successfully without duplicate indexed versions or objects.
  • Add API-key-protected POST /api/v2/admin/reconcile, returning JSON that identifies removed orphan objects and hidden versions missing a nupkg. It reclaims expired writes, removes unowned objects even if no claim or row exists, and removes broken versions from flat-container, registration and database search listings without affecting healthy versions. Recovery of expired uploads permits a fresh push. A deleted version leaves no version-prefix objects.

Keep existing packages from the old bucket layout ({id}.{version}.nupkg and {id}.nuspec under the same version prefix) readable, deletable and overwritable without reupload. Existing push, v3 download, registration, relist and hard-delete routes remain available. An existing PostgreSQL schema must upgrade in place, treating its rows as committed. A duplicate push of a non-overwritable version returns 409; push and delete routes, including relist, retain API-key protection (401 without a valid key). For a package containing only a nuspec, a committed version has exactly one owned nupkg and one owned nuspec object under its version prefix, including after a successful overwrite or reconciliation; abandoned attempts must not leave extra objects there.

The source is at /app. Build and run with dotnet build src/BaGetter/BaGetter.csproj -p:NuGetAudit=false from /app. PostgreSQL is postgres:5432, S3 is s3:4566 (S3-compatible LocalStack with path-style requests); both are provided as sidecars and the container has no Docker daemon. The deployment uses Database__Type=PostgreSql, Storage__Type=AwsS3, Search__Type=Database, AllowPackageOverwrites=PrereleaseOnly, and PackageDeletionBehavior=HardDelete; cold-mirror requests use Mirror__Enabled=true with a configured Mirror__PackageSource. Application settings use Database__ConnectionString, Storage__Endpoint, Storage__Bucket, Storage__AccessKey, Storage__SecretKey, Storage__ForcePathStyle, and ApiKey. The deployment database is sd with app-role credentials app/app; the S3 bucket is packages with credentials test/test, path-style access enabled, and the API key is secret (sent as X-NuGet-ApiKey). The app has no internet access.

Executive summary

Each task gives the agent a codebase that misbehaves and a description of the symptoms or the documentation it should follow. The agent finds the faulty code, fixes it without breaking what already works, and in some tasks writes a report naming each root cause. The main languages are Python (84%), Go (6%) and Rust (4%).

Gemini 4 Argon passes 25% of its runs and fails every run on 71% of them. Gemini 3.8 Flash passes 7% of its runs and fails every run on 67% of them.

Why this catalog

Problems engineers face

Maintainers are handed code that is wrong in several places and must find the causes without a test suite to lean on. In the diagnosis tasks, many undocumented edits break unrelated features at once. In the documentation-drift tasks, the code still runs but contradicts its own documentation. One task starts from a single production symptom with a hidden root cause.

How the tasks reproduce them

Each task ships a pinned checkout of an open-source project, with the tests withheld and no network. The prompt describes the symptoms or names the documentation in scope, never the location of the faults. Most diagnosis tasks also ask for /app/rca.json, which lists the file and function of each edit and is compared with an answer key. Drift tasks treat the documentation as the authority and forbid editing it. Hidden tests check the repairs and the behaviour that was already correct.

Typical prompts

  • A first-person list of symptoms grouped by feature, with no file or function named, ending in a request to fix and report.
  • A stated number of undocumented edits and a JSON schema for the root-cause report.
  • A library description with the source paths and documentation pages in scope, and the rule that documentation outranks code.

The repository at /workdir is Exo, a Python-embedded language and compiler for writing high-performance kernels. Procedures written in Exo object code (@proc, @instr, @config) are parsed, type-checked and bounds-checked, rewritten by user-scheduling primitives (loop and scope, buffer, configuration, sub-procedure, memory/precision/parallelism and other operations) that are addressed through cursors and patterns, and compiled to C (exocc, compile_procs, Procedure.c_code_str), with user-defined memories, instructions and externs and a standard library of higher-level scheduling and inspection functions.

Fix all implementation drift from the documentation in this repository. The code under repair is the Exo package src/exo except the platform instruction libraries in src/exo/platforms/. The documentation in scope is: README.md, every page under docs/ (including docs/primitives/), and the module, class and function docstrings of the in-scope modules of src/exo, including their examples.

Where the code and the documentation disagree about runtime behavior, the documentation is the authority: change the implementation so that it does what the documentation says, and do not edit or delete documentation to make a disagreement go away. The documentation is those pages and those docstrings; in-package code comments are only supporting evidence, and when a comment conflicts with the documentation, follow the documentation.

The environment runs Python 3.12 with PySMT, z3-solver, asdl-adt, yapf and pytest, and has no network access; exo is imported from /workdir/src. Keep the public API stable and keep every behavior that already matches its documentation working exactly as it does now.

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)

Diverged runs come out on top of our sweep CSV

We run our hyperparameter sweeps in local mode with the CSVWriter plugin and pick the winner by sorting swanlab_runs.csv on the final val/loss. The runs that blew up near the end (loss going to NaN in the last epochs) show up in that CSV with a val/loss of 0.0, so they sort straight to the top. We only caught it because last week's "best" learning rate turned out to have diverged. In swanlab watch the same runs do end in NaN, like they should.

The checkout is in /workdir. Could you track down where this actually goes wrong and fix it there? Please include a regression test, somewhere under tests/ (say tests/test_repro.py), that fails on the current code because of this problem (a real test failure, not an import error) and passes once it's fixed. Test the reported behaviour, not your patch: it should still pass if the bug gets fixed some other correct way, so no asserting on source text or on helpers only your fix has. It should run on its own from a clean checkout with just your test files added.

I doubt I'm the only one hitting this. Anything else that goes through that code is probably wrong too, so please fix it at the source rather than special-casing my input. The fix belongs in the library itself, not in the tests. CI runs the full test suite on every change, so it shouldn't break anything else.

When you're done, leave a short root-cause note at /workdir/rca.json:

{
  "root_causes": [{"file": "path/from/repo/root.py", "function": "Class.method"}],
  "reproducer": "tests/test_repro.py"
}

root_causes lists the function(s) where the problem actually starts (one or more), not where it shows up: the file relative to the repo root and the name as function or Class.method. Don't pad the list with functions that only pass the bad value along; extra entries count against the note. reproducer is the repo-relative path of your regression test.

Each task asks the agent to add a capability to an existing open-source library or service, specified as the public types and functions to deliver. The data pipeline tasks extend data libraries so pipelines keep producing correct results after an upstream format or schema change. The main languages are Go (68%), Python (32%) and C# (1%).

Gemini 4 Argon passes 11% of its runs and fails every run on 85% of them. Gemini 3.8 Flash passes <1% of its runs and fails every run on 98% of them.

Why this catalog

Problems engineers face

Maintainers add a capability that runs through many code paths of an unfamiliar library or service, while existing callers must see no change. Typical requests add an opt-in mode or policy, keep information the library currently drops, or make a subsystem safe under concurrency and failure.

Data engineers face a related problem: after an upstream format or schema change, a pipeline keeps running but produces wrong results. The library has to handle the new data while old inputs still work.

How the tasks reproduce them

Each task pins an open-source repository, mostly Go or Python, in an offline container and gives a written specification of the new behaviour. The agent's edits are collected as a diff against the base commit. After the session, hidden acceptance tests check the new behaviour and the project's existing tests check that nothing else changed. The data pipeline tasks also provide sample inputs in /data.

Typical prompts

  • A capability gap stated as "X cannot Y", then dense paragraphs on the behaviour to add and the behaviour to preserve.
  • A bullet list of required exported names, constants and signatures, with a research and plan file due before any code change.
  • A first-person data problem after an upstream change, with sample files in /data and a request to keep existing results unchanged.

Full instruction given to the agent (instruction.md)

I'm restoring transaction and query support in our copy of go-memdb so callers can update data, query snapshots, and watch query results for updates. Could you implement the methods that currently panic in the root memdb package? They live in txn.go, memdb.go, index.go, filter.go, and watch.go. The missing pieces cover transaction lifecycle, deletion, indexed queries and iteration, snapshots, deferred callbacks, filtering, and watch sets.

The existing code, API comments, and README.md provide context for the restoration. A received value must wake WatchCtx just as a closed watched channel does. Please keep the restored public names and signatures unchanged, and retain Txn.write for package compatibility; private helper functions are up to you. I'll check the restored behavior alongside index and schema regressions. Submit text Go source changes without new symbolic links, binary Go diffs, or Go line-position directives (//line and /*line). Use Go filenames that produce unquoted, whitespace-free paths in Git diffs.

In the non-test code you add, please avoid: new init() functions; the syscall, golang.org/x/sys, os/exec, os/signal, plugin, embed, runtime/cgo, runtime/pprof, runtime/trace, testing and flag packages, cgo, and //go:linkname or //go:embed directives; os.Exit, os.StartProcess, os.FindProcess and runtime.Goexit; reading os.Args, os.Executable, /proc/self or runtime/debug build info; caller or stack lookups (runtime.Caller, Callers, CallersFrames, FuncForPC, Stack, debug.Stack, debug.PrintStack, log.Lshortfile, log.Llongfile, and AddSource selectors or identifier keys); literal U+0016 or the text \x16; and printing test-runner lines such as --- PASS. These are rejected outright. Some checks read raw text and also match comments.

We track SQLite tables with sqlite-history-json (/app) and have since changed some: columns added with ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN, columns and tables renamed with ALTER TABLE RENAME while tracking was on, and columns dropped by disabling tracking, dropping and enabling again. Now restore returns NULLs or fails with "no such column" and history on a renamed table fails, but python -m sqlite_history_json.upgrade says there's nothing to upgrade. A copy of the database is at /data/shop.db.

After the upgrade, restoring a table that has tracking on to its latest entry should give exactly its current rows, and later changes should be recorded as on a table tracked from scratch. Existing entries keep their id, timestamp, operation, primary key and group, with each value under the current name of the column it was recorded from, in history, row-history, restore and row-state-sql. Values for dropped columns stay in the history and restore ignores them. A renamed table's history follows it, so everything works under the new name, enable and disable included.

Tables with tracking off and history of dropped tables stay as they are. A second run changes nothing. With --dry-run it lists only the tables it would change and changes nothing. If a renamed table's new name already has its own history, the upgrade exits with an error naming the table and changes nothing. Databases from 0.3 and earlier must still upgrade, and the tests in /app/tests must keep passing.

Could you find what's wrong and fix it? There's no network here.
